content: SUNY Downstate Medical Center, officially known as the State University of New York Health Science Center at Brooklyn, is a distinguished academic medical institution and the only one of its kind in Brooklyn, New York City. Its origins trace back to 1858 when the Long Island College Hospital was granted permission by the state to establish a medical school, marking it as the first hospital-based medical school in the United States. In 1931, the institution was rechartered as the Long Island College of Medicine. On April 5, 1950, it officially became Downstate following a merger between the Long Island College of Medicine and the newly formed State University of New York system. SUNY Downstate Medical Center comprises several academic and clinical entities, including the College of Medicine, College of Health Related Professions, College of Nursing, School of Graduate Studies, and the University Hospital of Brooklyn. The institution currently enrolls 1,516 students, with 50% of them being minorities or recent immigrants. Notably, the College of Medicine at SUNY Downstate has the highest percentage of minority students among all medical schools in New York State. The current president of the institution is Dr. John C. LaRosa. SUNY Downstate Medical Center holds several educational distinctions. It was the first hospital-based medical school in the United States and pioneered the first hospital-based nurse-midwifery training program in the country. Additionally, it established the first bachelor's degree program in medical sonography. Nationally, SUNY Downstate ranks eighth in the number of alumni who serve as faculty members at American medical schools. Among the nearly 21,000 physicians practicing in New York City, more graduated from SUNY Downstate than from any other medical school. Economically, SUNY Downstate Medical Center is a significant contributor to the Brooklyn community, being the fifth-largest employer in the borough. Approximately 85% of its employees reside in New York City, with 62% living in Brooklyn. The institution's total economic impact on New York State exceeds $627 million annually. For every dollar invested by the state, SUNY Downstate generates more than $12 in economic returns. Graduates of its nursing and allied health programs experience an increase in lifetime earning potential ranging from $288,000 to $925,000. In the 1998-1999 fiscal year, SUNY Downstate attracted $33.7 million in external research funding, including $24 million from federal sources. The institution has achieved numerous milestones in medical research. In 1955, Dr. Clarence Dennis, the inventor of the heart-lung machine, performed the first successful open-heart surgery in New York State. In 1964, Dr. Eli Friedman established the nation's first federally funded dialysis program at the University Hospital of Brooklyn. In 1977, Dr. Raymond Damadian produced the first human images using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). In 1984, Dr. Henri Begleiter published a groundbreaking study demonstrating that children of alcoholics may have an increased risk of developing alcoholism. In 1986, SUNY Downstate conducted the first federally funded study on the transmission of HIV from mother to fetus. In 1998, Dr. Robert Furchgott, a distinguished professor emeritus of pharmacology, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on nitric oxide. In 2006, Drs. Todd Sacktor and Andre Fenton conducted research on the maintenance of long-term potentiation and its implications for spatial memory storage, which was recognized as one of the top scientific breakthroughs of the year by Science magazine. In popular culture, SUNY Downstate Medical Center is referenced in Mos Def's 1999 song Got, where he mentions you takin' a ride on the Downstate Medical, alluding to the possibility of a victim of a violent robbery being transported to SUNY Downstate for medical care.
